chunks: And from him, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, both together, from Ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Al-Fudayl ibn Yasar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:

Regarding a slave who injured a free man, he said: If the free man desires, he can take retaliation from him; and if he desires, he can seize him, if the injury exceeds his freedom price, and if it does not exceed his freedom price, his master ransoms him. So if his master refuses to ransom him, there is for the injured free man from the slave an amount equal to the blood money of his injury, and the remainder is for the master. The slave is sold, so the injured man takes his right, and the remainder is returned to the master.

key_terms.افْتَدَاهُ: He ransomed him (paid to free him from the master's ownership)
key_terms.دِيَة: Blood money (compensation for injury or death)
key_terms.رَقَبَتِهِ: His freedom price (value of the slave)

ai.seo_question: What are the legal options for a free man when a slave injures him according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the jurisprudence of 'ta'abud' (subjugation) where a free man injures a slave, granting the free victim the choice between exacting retaliation (qisas) or accepting compensation (diya). It highlights the master's right to ransom the slave to avoid partial loss, reflecting the socio-legal hierarchy of early Islamic society where the slave's value was tied to the injury's severity relative to the free man's status. The ruling ensures that if the master refuses ransom, the slave is sold to satisfy the free man's claim, with the remainder returning to the master, illustrating the balance between retributive justice and property rights in Shia fiqh.

en.hubeali: And from him, and Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, both together from Ibn Mahboub, from Ali Bin Raib, from Al Fuzayl Bin Yasaar,

(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said regarding a salve having injured a free: ‘If the free one so desires to he can retaliate from it, and if he so desires to he can seize him, if it was such that the injuries exceeded his freedom (price), and if it did not exceed his freedom price, his master has to ransom him. So if his master refuses to ransom him, there would be for the free one, the injured, a wergild of the measure of his injuries sustained, and the remainder would be for the master. The slave would be sold, so the injured would take his right, and return the remainder upon the master’.
